checks.location: Proposition1 Eq12 and AppendixA unconditional Gaussian calculation versus actual conditioned/iMF parameter-gradient noise
checks.claim: Therefore, gradient variance is bounded and independent of data, and does not grow as the latent representation becomes more expressive or the conditioning becomes more complex.
checks.explanation: The displayed covariance is correct for the unconditional Gaussian interpolation in Appendix A. Parameter gradients also multiply target noise by the trainable model Jacobian. Conditioning on history or actions additionally changes the conditional target law, even when its marginal is exactly Gaussian.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(d=1\), \(\tau=1/2\), and \(Z_0,Z_1\) be independent standard Gaussians. Then \(\operatorname{Var}(V\mid Z_\tau)=2\) and the optimal unconditional predictor is zero. For the valid parametrization \(f_\theta=a\theta\), at \(\theta=0\),
\[
\nabla_\theta(f_\theta-V)^2=-2aV,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\nabla_\theta\ell\mid Z_\tau)=8a^2.
\]

The scale \(a\) is arbitrary while all latent distributions stay unchanged.

For the conditioning issue, keep the same Gaussian marginal and let \(C=\mathbf1_{\{|Z_1|>2\}}\). At \(\tau=0\), the target variance given \(Z_0,C=1\) is \(1+2\phi(2)/(1-\Phi(2))>5\), rather than the unconditional value \(1\).
checks.repair:
State Eq. (12) as the unconditional independent-Gaussian velocity-target covariance. For a squared-loss predictor with inputs \(I\) and Jacobian \(J\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\nabla_\theta\ell\mid I)
=4J^\top\operatorname{Cov}(V\mid I)J.
\]

If \(\|J\|_{\rm op}\leq L\) uniformly, conditional total variance and Eq. (12) imply the averaged irreducible gradient-noise bound
\[
\mathbb E\|\nabla_\theta\ell-\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta\ell\mid I]\|^2\leq8L^2d.
\]

The explicit Jacobian condition is essential. The self-dependent iMF target requires a separate argument.
checks.scope: Eq. (12) correctly gives the independent-Gaussian velocity covariance. The replacement bound concerns averaged irreducible squared-loss gradient noise and requires a uniform bound on model sensitivity.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 1 computes the conditional velocity-target covariance for independent standard Gaussian endpoints. It concludes that gradient variance is bounded and independent of data, representation expressivity and conditioning complexity.
checks.title: A velocity-target covariance bound does not bound arbitrary parameter gradients
checks.whyItMatters: Latent marginal regularization alone does not control how model parameters amplify target noise.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.2, Proposition 1 and Eq. (12); Appendix A, Eqs. (19)–(28) (arXiv v1)

checks.location: Proposition2 Eq15 and AppendixA Eq31 substitution of random sample U for population tr(Sigma)/d
checks.claim: By the maximum entropy theorem, the predictive entropy is upper-bounded by a function of $\mathcal{U}$ as
checks.explanation: Unbiasedness gives \(\mathbb E[U\mid x,c]=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_c)/d\). It does not make the random value equal to that population variance. The maximum-entropy argument bounds entropy using the population covariance.
checks.demonstration:
Use \(d=1\), constant uninformative context, exact predictive law \(N(0,1)\), and two independent predictions. Then
\[
U=(Y_1-Y_2)^2/2\sim\chi^2_1,\qquad H(Y)=\tfrac12\log(2\pi e).
\]

The claimed inequality requires \(U\geq1\). It fails with probability \(\Pr(\chi^2_1<1)\approx0.682689\). An open neighborhood of samples \((-1/4,1/4)\) already violates it, so the witness has positive probability.
checks.repair:
With \(v=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_c)/d=\mathbb E[U\mid x,c]\), maximum entropy and eigenvalue AM–GM prove
\[
H(Z\mid x,c)\leq\frac d2\log(2\pi e\,v).
\]

A finite-sample version is available under the additional assumption of an isotropic Gaussian predictive law \(N(\mu,\sigma^2I_d)\). For \(\nu=d(N-1)\), \(\nu U/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_\nu\). If \(q_{\nu,\delta}\) is its lower-tail \(\delta\) quantile, then with probability at least \(1-\delta\),
\[
H(Z\mid x,c)\leq\frac d2\log\left(2\pi e\,\frac{\nu U}{q_{\nu,\delta}}\right).
\]

This confidence statement needs the predictive-law assumption; a Gaussian latent marginal alone does not supply it for every context.
checks.scope: The population entropy upper bound is valid. The finite random plug-in assertion fails even for perfect Gaussian predictions; the corrected confidence bound is a restricted replacement.
checks.title: An unbiased sample variance does not give a guaranteed entropy upper bound
checks.claimContext: Proposition 2 assumes independent predictions from a well-trained model, defines \(U\) as the mean unbiased sample variance, and uses the observed finite-ensemble value in an upper bound on conditional predictive entropy.
checks.whyItMatters: A small finite ensemble can underestimate variance and thereby put the asserted upper bound below the true entropy.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.3, Proposition 2, Eqs. (13)–(15); Appendix A, Eqs. (29)–(32) (arXiv v1)

checks.location: Proposition2 bounded scale U in[0,1] versus AppendixA Eq33 expected conditional covariance statement
checks.claim: Furthermore, $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded within $[0,1]$ , providing an interpretable absolute scale.
checks.explanation: Sample variance has unbounded support for Gaussian predictions. Moreover, context-specific population variance can exceed the marginal variance. Total covariance controls an average across contexts.
checks.demonstration:
With exact \(N(0,1)\) predictions and two rollouts, \(U\sim\chi^2_1\). Therefore \(\Pr(U>1)\approx0.317311\), and there is positive probability above every finite threshold.

Even the population limit can exceed one. Let \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), \(C=\mathbf1_{\{|Z|>2\}}\). Then
\[
\mathbb E[Z\mid C=1]=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid C=1)=1+\frac{2\phi(2)}{1-\Phi(2)}\approx5.74643.
\]

The marginal remains exactly standard Gaussian.
checks.repair:
Keep nonnegativity and state the averaged scale. For exact marginal covariance \(I_d\), total covariance gives
\[
\mathbb E_C\operatorname{Cov}(Z\mid C)
=I_d-\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb E[Z\mid C])\preceq I_d,
\]
so \(\mathbb E_{C,\mathrm{samples}}U\leq1\). This is exact under the unit marginal assumption; approximate marginal regularization gives the corresponding approximate average. Clipping at one would define a different estimator and would not repair the entropy bound.
checks.scope: The lower bound is valid. The upper bound is valid only as the stated cross-context expectation, not for an individual context or ensemble.
checks.title: Unit marginal variance gives an average scale, not an upper endpoint
checks.claimContext: After defining finite-ensemble uncertainty \(U\), Proposition 2 states that it lies in the absolute interval \([0,1]\). Appendix A invokes total covariance under a unit Gaussian latent marginal.
checks.whyItMatters: The value one cannot serve as a universal maximum predictive-uncertainty level.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.3, Proposition 2, Eq. (13) and bounded-scale statement; Appendix A, Eq. (33) (arXiv v1)

checks.location: Remark2 Eqs16-17 deterministic continuous seed mutual information and zero conditional entropy argument
checks.claim: Therefore, $\mathcal{U}$ is a proxy motivated by EIG, and maximizing $\mathcal{U}$ approximately maximizes an upper bound on EIG.
checks.explanation: The argument combines discrete deterministic conditional entropy with a continuous differential-entropy bound. A non-atomic output determined exactly by its continuous seed has a singular joint law and infinite mutual information in the invertible-flow example.
checks.demonstration:
Take the identity flow \(Z_1=Z_0\sim N(0,1)\), a valid deterministic Gaussian-to-Gaussian ODE map. The joint law is concentrated on the diagonal, which has zero probability under the product of the two Gaussian marginals. Consequently
\[
I(Z_0;Z_1)=+\infty,\qquad
h(Z_1)=\tfrac12\log(2\pi e)<\infty.
\]

Equivalently, partition the Gaussian into \(k\) equal-probability bins. Data processing yields \(I(Z_0;Z_1)\geq\log k\) for every \(k\). Given the seed, the output law is a Dirac measure; its differential entropy is not zero.
checks.repair:
A finite information objective requires a specified finite-resolution or noisy observation. For example, if \(Y=F(Z_0)+\epsilon\) with independent \(\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma_n^2I_d)\), then maximum entropy gives
\[
I(Z_0;Y)\leq\frac d2\log\left(1+\frac{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}(F(Z_0))}{d\sigma_n^2}\right).
\]

This is a proved statement for a changed observation model. It does not establish the paper's finite EIG for the deterministic continuous output. No repair preserving that original information identity is established here.
checks.scope: The finding concerns the finite EIG identity and its upper-bound motivation. Predictive spread can still be used as a heuristic planning bonus.
checks.claimContext: Remark 2 treats the continuous Gaussian seed as a world seed, assigns zero conditional entropy to the deterministic flow output given that seed, and identifies finite predictive differential entropy with seed-output EIG.
checks.title: A deterministic continuous flow has infinite seed-output information
checks.whyItMatters: The stated information-theoretic justification fails even with exact Gaussian latents and an exact flow.

checks.claim: EpicWorldModel draws N rollouts (FM: 10 NFE; iMF: 2 NFE) and scores mean goal $MSE-\beta U$ , both z-score normalised across candidates.

Use \(d=1\), \(N=2\), \(z_g=0\), and \(\beta=0.4\). Candidate rollouts are
\[
A=(1,1),\quad
B=(\sqrt{1.5}+\sqrt{0.5},\,\sqrt{1.5}-\sqrt{0.5}),\quad
C=(10,10).
\]

Their mean squared goal losses are \(E=(1,2,100)\) and unbiased variances are \(U=(0,1,0)\). Eq. (18) gives costs \((2,3.6,200)\), selecting \(A\). The normalized objective gives

Specify the normalized mean objective explicitly, including a convention for zero candidate variance. If MSE averages \(N\) rollouts and \(d\) coordinates, the raw goal term is \(NdE\). For one fixed batch, separate z-scores are equivalent to

Matching the raw objective requires \(\beta_{\rm raw}=Nd\,\beta_{\rm norm}\sigma_E/\sigma_U\), a batch-dependent conversion. This algebra establishes the relation between the two specifications.

checks.claim: this expectation is a Monte Carlo estimate of $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\geq 0$
checks.explanation: The sum of token log ratios is the sequence log ratio. A response-dependent inverse length reweights outcomes and can make its exact on-policy expectation negative. This is a population issue, not merely a noisy negative sample.
checks.demonstration:
Consider two completed responses. \(A\) is immediate EOS, of length one; \(B\) emits one other token and then deterministic EOS, of length two. Let the first-step branch probabilities be
\[
\pi_\theta=(1/2,1/2),\qquad \pi_{\rm ref}=(3/4,1/4).
\]

Both models have the same support. Later conditional token ratios equal one. Thus
\[
\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}\frac{\log(\pi_\theta(Y)/\pi_{\rm ref}(Y))}{T(Y)}
=\tfrac12\log(2/3)+\tfrac14\log2\approx-0.029446.
\]

The true sequence KL is \(\tfrac12\log(2/3)+\tfrac12\log2\approx0.143841>0\).
checks.repair: Sum the token log ratios per on-policy sequence to estimate sequence KL. A common fixed response length \(L\) gives the nonnegative value \(\operatorname{KL}/L\). Alternatively specify a context distribution and average exact conditional-token KLs over it. The aggregate token average converges to sequence KL divided by expected length, a different operation from averaging response-level token means.
checks.scope: The population expectation can be negative under the on-policy sampling specified in arXiv v2. The correction concerns the divergence interpretation of response-length normalization.
checks.claimContext: Section 4.4 explicitly uses on-policy rollouts. Eq. (8) averages token log policy/reference ratios within each response, then claims its expectation estimates a nonnegative KL divergence.

checks.location: AppendixE Proposition2; aggregate gradient
checks.claim: Only the losses $\ell_{i}$ with $i\in\mathcal{A}(j)$ depend on $s_{j}$
checks.explanation: The node's own loss depends on its score whenever it has descendants. That term supplies its upward preference pressure and can change the sign of the total derivative.
checks.demonstration:
For a two-node edge \(1\to2\) at equal scores, the actual gradient is \((-1/2,1/2)\). The printed formula assigns zero to the top node.

For a three-node layered chain at zero scores, the middle derivative is
\[
\frac13+\frac12-1=-\frac16,
\]
whereas the printed ancestor sum is \(1/3\). Also, adding a common constant to all scores leaves the objective unchanged; its total gradient must sum to zero. The ancestor-only positive formula violates that requirement.
checks.repair:
The correct derivative for the Appendix's unnormalized sum is
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\rm graph}}{\partial s_j}
=\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(j)}p_i(j)+p_j(j)-1
=\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(j)}p_i(j)-\sum_{k\in\mathcal N^-(j)}p_j(k).
\]

This follows by differentiating every local log-sum-exp. A global averaging factor multiplies all terms together. The ancestor sum remains a valid incoming contribution, and equals the full derivative for a sink.
checks.scope: The local edge derivative and the GraphDPO objective remain valid. Ancestor-count arguments must apply to the incoming component rather than an unqualified signed total update.
checks.claimContext: Appendix E defines \(\ell_i=-s_i+\log\sum_{k\in\{i\}\cup\mathcal N^-(i)}e^{s_k}\). Proposition 2 says only ancestor losses depend on \(s_j\), and identifies the total derivative with their positive contributions.
checks.title: The total score gradient also includes the node's own loss
checks.whyItMatters: Omitting the own-node term can predict the wrong update direction for an internal preference node.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix E, Implicit edge weighting, Proposition 2 and Gradient-based characterization (arXiv v2)

checks.location: AppendixE Corollary1
checks.claim: Under layered graphs, GraphDPO induces uniform weighting across all edges between any pair of groups, while assigning higher aggregate weight to comparisons involving lower-ranked groups.
checks.explanation: Same-group source nodes share dominated sets, but their local denominators include different self scores. Destination nodes can also have different policy scores despite tied preferences. Ancestor counts alone do not compare the resulting softmax sums.
checks.demonstration:
For classes \(\{a,b\}>\{c,d\}\), use exponentiated scores proportional to \((1,2,3,4)\). At \(\beta=1\), these are realized by a uniform reference and policy probabilities \((0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4)\), up to a common score shift. Then
\[
p_a(c)=3/8,\qquad p_b(c)=3/9,\qquad p_a(d)=4/8,
\]
so weights differ within the same class pair.

Even scores aligned with rank do not guarantee stronger incoming pressure for lower ranks. For three singleton layers with exponentiated scores \((100,1,0.001)\), middle incoming weight is about \(0.009901\), while bottom incoming weight is about \(0.001009\), despite its larger ancestor set.
checks.repair:
Equal model scores within each class are sufficient for equal weights between a given pair of classes: the source denominators and destination numerators then agree. If all scores are equal, the incoming weight of a node in class \(h\) is
\[
\sum_{g<h}\frac{|\mathcal C_g|}{1+\sum_{\ell>g}|\mathcal C_\ell|},
\]
which increases with \(h\) for nonempty classes. This proves the interpretation in an explicit restricted regime. Generally retain the exact adaptive edge weights and degree-modulated bounds; preference ties alone supply neither conclusion.
checks.scope: The counterexamples concern incoming edge weights after the own-node term is included in the total gradient. The layered loss remains unchanged.
checks.claimContext: Appendix E Corollary 1 asserts uniform edge weighting between layered preference groups and increasing aggregate weight for lower-ranked groups. Equal preference rank does not impose equal model log-ratio scores.
checks.title: Preference ties do not imply uniform policy-softmax edge weights
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed uniform weighting and rank-based pressure are not universal properties of the objective.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix E, Corollary 1 and proof; Proposition 2's ancestor-weight interpretation (arXiv v2)

checks.repair: Include the fixed schema’s maximum arity when translating fact-degree to value adjacency and deriving the neighborhood bound.
checks.scope: The explicit constant is wrong; fixed-schema finiteness and the corresponding asymptotic argument remain possible.
